text: I have a theory that you can tell everything about a marriage by the way two people load a dishwasher. My husband believes the dishwasher is a suggestion, a kind of loose architectural guideline, and that bowls may be placed wherever the spirit moves them. I believe the dishwasher is a covenant. There is a correct way, which is my way, and there is chaos, which is everyone else's. For eleven years I reloaded it after him every single night, silently, like a saint, except that saints don't slam the silverware basket. Then one day I stopped. I let the plates emerge spotted and faintly soapy and I said nothing, and I felt enormous, like a woman who has finally let go of something. This lasted four days. On the fifth day I was back at the dishwasher at eleven at night in my nightgown, rearranging the mugs, and I understood at last that I had not married a man who loads dishwashers wrong. I had married a dishwasher, and the man came with it, and there was no return policy on either.

My mother had exactly one piece of advice about cooking, which was that you should never apologize for the food, and exactly one piece of advice about everything else, which was that you should always apologize first so the other person couldn't. I have spent my whole life trying to reconcile these. I throw dinner parties at which I serve a slightly underdone chicken with total confidence and then apologize, preemptively and at length, for the state of the bathroom, the weather, my hair, and the fact that I have invited these particular people to sit next to each other. The chicken is fine. The chicken is always fine. It is everything around the chicken that I cannot leave alone. Last week a guest told me the meal was perfect, and instead of saying thank you I heard myself explain that the napkins were supposed to match. She looked at me the way you look at someone backing slowly off a curb. I come from a long line of women who could not accept a compliment without immediately renovating it. We are wonderful cooks. We are terrible guests at our own tables.

The summer I turned forty I decided to become a person who exercised. I bought the shoes. The shoes are the part everyone gets right; it's the using of them that falls apart. I had a whole plan involving a reservoir and a sports bra and a sense of myself as someone glimpsed jogging at dawn, lean and purposeful, the kind of woman other women resent on principle. What actually happened is that I went twice. The first time I ran for nine minutes and walked home composing the eulogy I felt I had earned. The second time it rained, which I took as a sign, because I take everything as a sign when the sign is telling me to go back to bed. The shoes lived by the door for a year, accusatory, gathering the particular dust that only aspirational objects gather. Eventually I gave them to my sister, who actually runs, and who thanked me as though I'd given her something of mine, when really I'd given her something of the woman I had briefly, expensively, agreed not to become.

I keep a drawer of things I am saving for good. There is a candle in it shaped like a pear that I have owned since the Clinton administration. There is a bar of French soap that has fused, over the decades, to its own wrapper, so that the soap and the idea of the soap are now a single archaeological object. There is a bottle of perfume I was given by a man I no longer speak to, which I cannot wear because of him and cannot throw away because of how good it smells, a contradiction I have decided not to examine too closely. The drawer is a museum of occasions that never arrived, of the better, calmer, more deserving version of me who would eventually be worthy of a pear-shaped candle. I am sixty-one. I think it is finally time to admit that she is not coming, that there is no good occasion out there waiting, that this Tuesday, with its leftover soup and its unanswered email, is the occasion. So tonight I am lighting the pear. It probably smells like 1996. I find I am completely fine with that.

We bought the apartment for the light, which is what people say when they have paid too much money for a place with a problem they haven't found yet. The light was real. At four o'clock in October it came through the front windows and turned the whole living room the color of a peach, and you forgot, in that light, that the radiators clanked like a man being beaten with a pipe and that the previous owner had, for reasons known only to God, tiled the kitchen in a green that can only be described as institutional. I loved that apartment the way you love a difficult person: completely, and against my own interests. We fixed the radiators. We re-tiled the kitchen. We sanded and painted and argued about paint in the specialized vocabulary that couples develop solely in order to argue about paint. And then one afternoon I stood in the finished, perfected, four-o'clock light and realized we had spent two years and a great deal of money turning the place we fell in love with into a place we would now have to fall in love with all over again. We did, eventually. But it took longer than the tiling.
